elements.name: Hydrogen
facts: Isolated by reacting acids with metals and recognizing a flammable gas lighter than air.
Makes up about 75% of the universe's ordinary matter by mass.
Combines with oxygen to form water — the origin of its name.

elements.name: Helium
facts: First spotted as a yellow spectral line in sunlight during an 1868 eclipse.
About 24% of the universe's ordinary matter by mass, second after hydrogen.
Named for the Sun because it was found there before being found on Earth.

elements.name: Lithium
facts: Discovered in the mineral petalite.
Lightest metal and a key ingredient in rechargeable batteries.
Used medically as a mood-stabilizing salt.

elements.name: Beryllium
facts: Isolated from beryl and emerald ores.
Very stiff and light — used in aerospace alloys.
Dust is highly toxic if inhaled.

elements.name: Boron
elements.discoveredBy: Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac & Louis Jacques Thénard
facts: Prepared by reducing boric acid with potassium.
Essential for plant cell walls.
Borosilicate glass resists thermal shock.

elements.name: Carbon
facts: Basis of organic chemistry and all known life.
Forms diamond, graphite, graphene, and fullerenes.
Carbon-14 dating measures ages of once-living materials.

elements.name: Nitrogen
facts: About 78% of Earth's atmosphere by volume.
Essential in amino acids and the Haber–Bosch fertilizer process.
Liquid nitrogen cools to −196 °C.

elements.name: Oxygen
facts: Independently discovered; Lavoisier named it and explained combustion.
About 21% of air by volume and about 46% of Earth's crust by mass.
Ozone (O₃) in the stratosphere shields UV light.

elements.name: Fluorine
facts: Most reactive element; first isolated by electrolysis of potassium fluoride.
Added to toothpaste as fluoride to strengthen enamel.
Used in PTFE (Teflon) and many refrigerants.

elements.name: Neon
facts: Discovered by chilling air until the rare gases separated.
Glows red-orange in discharge tubes — classic neon signs.
Second-lightest noble gas.

elements.name: Sodium
elements.namedAfter: English soda; symbol from Latin natrium
facts: Isolated by electrolyzing molten soda (sodium hydroxide).
Vital electrolyte in nerve signals and table salt (NaCl).
Reacts violently with water.

elements.name: Magnesium
facts: Burns with a brilliant white flame.
Chlorophyll's central atom in green plants.
Lightweight structural metal in cars and aircraft.

elements.name: Aluminum
facts: Once rarer than gold until the Hall–Héroult process made it cheap.
Most abundant metal in Earth's crust, about 8% by mass.
Light, corrosion-resistant, endlessly recyclable.

elements.name: Silicon
facts: About 28% of Earth's crust by mass, second only to oxygen.
Heart of computer chips and solar cells.
Silica (SiO₂) forms quartz and sand.

elements.name: Phosphorus
facts: First isolated by boiling urine down to a glowing white solid.
Essential in DNA, ATP, and fertilizers.
White phosphorus ignites in air; red phosphorus is safer.

elements.name: Sulfur
facts: Found near volcanoes and hot springs.
Key in vulcanizing rubber and making sulfuric acid.
Smells of rotten eggs as hydrogen sulfide.

elements.name: Chlorine
facts: Greenish-yellow gas; Scheele made it from hydrochloric acid and manganese dioxide.
Disinfects drinking water and swimming pools.
Component of PVC plastic and table salt.

elements.name: Argon
facts: Discovered as an inert residue after removing N₂ and O₂ from air.
About 0.93% of Earth's atmosphere by volume.
Used to fill light bulbs and shield welding arcs.

elements.name: Potassium
elements.namedAfter: English potash; symbol from Latin kalium
facts: Isolated by electrolysis of potash.
Critical electrolyte for heart and nerve function.
Many common foods supply potassium.

elements.name: Calcium
facts: Isolated from lime by electrolysis.
Builds bones and teeth as calcium phosphate.
Limestone, chalk, and marble are calcium carbonate.

elements.name: Scandium
facts: Found in the minerals euxenite and gadolinite.
Light alloy additive for aerospace and sports gear.
Predicted by Mendeleev as eka-boron.

elements.name: Titanium
facts: Discovered in ilmenite sand in Cornwall.
Strong as steel but much lighter; resists corrosion.
Used in jet engines, implants, and white pigment (TiO₂).

elements.name: Vanadium
elements.discoveredBy: Andrés Manuel del Río (1801); rediscovered by Nils Gabriel Sefström
facts: Named for the colorful compounds it forms.
Strengthens steel for tools and pipelines.
Del Río's earlier brown lead discovery was overlooked.

elements.name: Chromium
facts: Gives emeralds their green and rubies their red.
Chrome plating and stainless steel both rely on it.
Essential trace nutrient in tiny amounts.

elements.name: Manganese
facts: Isolated by reducing pyrolusite with charcoal.
Removes oxygen and sulfur in steelmaking.
Critical in alkaline batteries and photosynthesis enzymes.

elements.name: Iron
elements.namedAfter: Anglo-Saxon iren; symbol from Latin ferrum
facts: Earth's core is about 85% iron, plus nickel and lighter elements.
Hemoglobin carries oxygen using iron.
Rust is iron oxide — a slow reverse of smelting.

elements.name: Cobalt
facts: Miners blamed kobolds when ores failed to yield copper.
Makes the deep blue of stained glass and ceramics.
Vital in vitamin B₁₂.

elements.name: Nickel
facts: Mistaken for copper ore that wouldn't smelt.
Major component of stainless steel and coins.
About 5 to 10% of Earth's core.

elements.name: Copper
facts: First metal widely worked by humans.
Excellent electrical conductor — wiring standard.
Statues and roofs slowly form green copper carbonate.

elements.name: Zinc
facts: Isolated by heating calamine with charcoal.
Galvanizes steel to prevent rust.
Essential for immune enzymes; deficiency causes slow healing.

elements.name: Gallium
facts: Predicted by Mendeleev as eka-aluminum.
Melts in your hand (29.8 °C).
Key semiconductor in LEDs and solar cells (GaAs).

elements.name: Germanium
facts: Predicted as eka-silicon by Mendeleev.
Early transistor semiconductor before silicon dominated.
Transparent to infrared — used in IR optics.

elements.name: Arsenic
facts: Infamous historical poison; still used carefully in semiconductors.
Gray arsenic is the stable metallic form.
Once common in pesticides and wood preservatives.

elements.name: Selenium
facts: Named as a counterpart to tellurium (Earth).
Photoconductive — used in early photocopiers.
Essential antioxidant nutrient in tiny doses; toxic in excess.

elements.name: Bromine
facts: Only nonmetallic element liquid at room temperature.
Reddish-brown vapor with a sharp smell.
Once used in flame retardants and photographic chemicals.

elements.name: Krypton
facts: Found as a hidden residue in liquefied air.
Used in high-intensity lamps and some lasers.
Defined the meter via a krypton-86 spectral line (1960–1983).

elements.name: Rubidium
facts: Named for deep-red spectral lines.
Soft metal that ignites spontaneously in air.
Used in atomic clocks and Bose–Einstein condensate research.

elements.name: Strontium
facts: Named for the village where strontianite was found.
Crimson-red fireworks and emergency flares.
Radioactive Sr-90 is a nuclear fallout concern.

elements.name: Yttrium
facts: One of four elements named for the Ytterby quarry.
Key in red phosphors for older TV screens.
Used in lasers (YAG) and superconductors.

elements.name: Zirconium
facts: Found in zircon gemstones.
Extremely corrosion-resistant cladding for nuclear fuel.
Cubic zirconia mimics diamond in jewelry.

elements.name: Niobium
facts: Originally called columbium in America.
Superconducting alloys for MRI magnets.
Named for Niobe, daughter of Tantalus — near twin of tantalum.

elements.name: Molybdenum
elements.discoveredBy: Carl Wilhelm Scheele (recognized); Peter Jacob Hjelm (isolated)
facts: Confused with lead ores until Scheele showed otherwise.
Toughens steel for armor and tools.
Essential enzyme cofactor in nitrogen fixation.

elements.name: Technetium
facts: First element discovered by artificial synthesis.
Filled a gap Mendeleev left in the table.
Tc-99m is the workhorse isotope of medical imaging.

elements.name: Ruthenium
facts: Isolated from Ural platinum ores.
Hardens platinum alloys for fountain-pen tips and contacts.
Catalyzes many industrial reactions.

elements.name: Rhodium
facts: Named for the rose-red color of its salts.
Catalytic converters and reflective mirrors.
Rarest and often most expensive precious metal.

elements.name: Palladium
facts: Discovered while purifying platinum.
Absorbs huge volumes of hydrogen.
Jewelry white gold alloys and catalytic converters.

elements.name: Silver
elements.namedAfter: Anglo-Saxon seolfor; symbol from Latin argentum
facts: Best electrical conductor of all metals.
Antimicrobial — used in wound dressings.
Historical basis of coinage and photography.

elements.name: Cadmium
facts: Found as an impurity in zinc carbonate.
Once common in NiCd batteries; now restricted for toxicity.
Brilliant yellow and red artist pigments (use carefully).

elements.name: Indium
facts: Named for a brilliant indigo line in its spectrum.
Soft enough to score with a fingernail.
Transparent indium tin oxide coats touchscreens.

elements.name: Tin
elements.namedAfter: Anglo-Saxon tin; symbol from Latin stannum
facts: Alloyed with copper to make bronze.
Tin cans are steel lined with tin to resist corrosion.
Tin cry is the crackling sound when a bar bends.

elements.name: Antimony
elements.namedAfter: Greek anti + monos; symbol from Latin stibium
facts: Stibnite was used as ancient eye makeup.
Hardens lead for bullets and battery plates.
Expands on freezing — useful in casting type metal.

elements.name: Tellurium
facts: Isolated from Transylvanian gold ores.
Improves machinability of steel and copper.
Cadmium telluride is used in thin-film solar panels.

elements.name: Iodine
facts: Discovered as violet vapor from seaweed ash.
Essential for thyroid hormones.
Tincture of iodine was a classic antiseptic.

elements.name: Xenon
facts: Rarest stable noble gas in air.
Bright white flash lamps and car HID headlights.
Forms real compounds — surprising for a noble gas.

elements.name: Cesium
facts: Named for sky-blue spectral lines.
Softest metal; melts near room temperature (28 °C).
Defines the second via cesium atomic clocks.

elements.name: Barium
facts: Isolated from heavy spar (baryte).
Barium meals make the gut visible on X-rays.
Green fireworks use barium salts.

elements.name: Lanthanum
facts: Hidden in cerium earth minerals for years.
First of the lanthanide series.
Used in camera lenses and nickel-metal hydride batteries.

elements.name: Cerium
facts: Most abundant rare-earth metal, about 0.006% of Earth's crust.
Cerium oxide polishes glass and catalyzes self-cleaning ovens.
Mischmetal lighter flints are mostly cerium.

elements.name: Praseodymium
facts: Split from didymium along with neodymium.
Green-yellow glass and high-power magnets.
Name means green twin.

elements.name: Neodymium
facts: Also split from didymium.
NdFeB magnets are the strongest common permanent magnets.
Purple glass and lasers use neodymium.

elements.name: Promethium
elements.discoveredBy: Jacob A. Marinsky, Lawrence E. Glendenin & Charles D. Coryell
facts: Only lanthanide with no stable isotopes.
First isolated from uranium fission products.
Named for the titan who stole fire — fitting for a nuclear-era find.

elements.name: Samarium
facts: Found spectroscopically in samarskite.
SmCo magnets stay strong at high temperature.
Used in control rods and cancer radiotherapy.

elements.name: Europium
facts: Most reactive rare-earth metal.
Red phosphor in TVs and euro banknote anti-counterfeit strips.
Named for the continent.

elements.name: Gadolinium
facts: Named for the Finnish chemist Gadolin.
Strongest elemental ferromagnet among rare earths near room temperature contexts.
MRI contrast agents historically used gadolinium complexes.

elements.name: Terbium
facts: Another Ytterby namesake.
Green phosphor in fluorescent lamps and TVs.
Magnetostrictive Terfenol-D uses terbium.

elements.name: Dysprosium
facts: Named for how difficult it was to isolate.
Boosts NdFeB magnets against demagnetization by heat.
Used in nuclear control rods.

elements.name: Holmium
facts: Named for Stockholm.
Highest magnetic moment of any naturally occurring element.
Holmium lasers cut bone and soft tissue in surgery.

elements.name: Erbium
facts: Third Ytterby element.
Erbium-doped fiber amplifiers power long-haul internet cables.
Pink erbium glass is a classic art glass color.

elements.name: Thulium
facts: Rarest of the stable lanthanides.
Portable X-ray devices once used thulium-170.
Named for the far-northern land of Thule.

elements.name: Ytterbium
facts: Fourth element named for Ytterby.
Atomic clocks and gravitational redshift experiments.
Improves stainless steel grain strength.

elements.name: Lutetium
facts: Last lanthanide discovered.
Hardest and densest rare-earth metal.
Lu-177 is used in targeted cancer radiotherapy.

elements.name: Hafnium
facts: Predicted by Mendeleev; found with zirconium.
Almost inseparable chemically from zirconium.
Nuclear control rods and high-k chip dielectrics.

elements.name: Tantalum
facts: Named for tantalizing chemists who couldn't dissolve it.
Capacitors in phones and laptops.
Extremely corrosion-resistant surgical implants.

elements.name: Tungsten
elements.namedAfter: Swedish tung sten (heavy stone); symbol from wolfram
facts: Highest melting point of all metals (3422 °C).
Incandescent bulb filaments made tungsten famous.
Wolframite ore gives the symbol W.

elements.name: Rhenium
elements.discoveredBy: Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke & Otto Berg
facts: Last stable element discovered.
Jet-engine superalloys and reforming catalysts.
Named for the Rhine River.

elements.name: Osmium
facts: Densest naturally occurring element.
Toxic osmium tetroxide has a sharp smell.
Hard alloy tips for fountain pens and electrical contacts.

elements.name: Iridium
facts: Named for colorful salts.
Extremely corrosion-resistant; spark plugs and crucibles.
Iridium layer marks the dinosaur-extinction asteroid impact.

elements.name: Platinum
elements.discoveredBy: Antonio de Ulloa (Europe); known earlier in S. America
facts: Catalytic converters, labware, and fine jewelry.
Does not tarnish — a noble metal.
Chemically akin to palladium and gold.

elements.name: Gold
elements.namedAfter: Anglo-Saxon gold; symbol from Latin aurum
facts: Does not corrode — found native in nature.
International monetary and cultural store of value.
Excellent conductor used in critical electronics.

elements.name: Mercury
elements.namedAfter: Mercury the planet/god; symbol from Latin hydrargyrum
facts: Only metal liquid at standard conditions.
Once used in thermometers and amalgams — now restricted for toxicity.
Name hydrargyrum means water-silver.

elements.name: Thallium
facts: Named for a bright green spectral line.
Highly toxic — once an infamous rat poison.
Specialized electronics and infrared optics.

elements.name: Lead
elements.namedAfter: Anglo-Saxon lead; symbol from Latin plumbum
facts: Soft, dense, and easy to cast — Roman plumbing (hence plumb).
Toxic to nerves; phased out of paint and gasoline.
Lead-acid batteries still dominate car starters.

elements.name: Bismuth
facts: Long mistaken for lead or tin.
Least toxic heavy metal; rainbow oxide crystals are popular.
Low-melting alloys for fire sprinklers and solders.

elements.name: Polonium
facts: Discovered while researching uranium ore pitchblende.
Marie Curie named it for her native Poland.
Intensely radioactive — used in antistatic devices and research.

elements.name: Astatine
elements.discoveredBy: Dale R. Corson, Kenneth Ross MacKenzie & Emilio Segrè
facts: Rarest naturally occurring element on Earth.
All isotopes are short-lived radioactives.
Synthesized by bombarding bismuth with alpha particles.

elements.name: Radon
facts: Colorless radioactive gas from radium's decay chain.
Indoor radon is a leading cause of lung cancer after smoking.
Heaviest noble gas.

elements.name: Francium
facts: Last element discovered in nature before synthetic-only finds.
Extremely rare and radioactive — seconds to minutes of half-life.
Perey found it as an actinium decay product at the Curie Institute.

elements.name: Radium
facts: Glowed in the dark — famously used on watch dials.
Curies processed tons of pitchblende to isolate a speck.
Radiation dangers were learned the hard way.

elements.name: Actinium
facts: First of the actinide series.
Glows pale blue in the dark from its own radioactivity.
Occurs in uranium ores in tiny amounts.

elements.name: Thorium
facts: About three to four times as common as uranium in Earth's crust.
Proposed as an alternative nuclear fuel cycle.
Once used in gas-mantle lanterns.

elements.name: Protactinium
elements.discoveredBy: Kasimir Fajans & Oswald Helmuth Göhring; isolated by Lise Meitner & Otto Hahn
facts: Name means it decays into actinium.
One of the rarest and most expensive naturally occurring elements.
Silvery metal that tarnishes in air.

elements.name: Uranium
facts: Named shortly after Uranus was discovered.
Fuel for nuclear reactors and weapons (enriched).
Natural uranium is mostly U-238 with about 0.7% fissile U-235.

elements.name: Neptunium
facts: First transuranium element synthesized.
Named to follow uranium, as Neptune follows Uranus.
Produced in nuclear reactors as a byproduct.

elements.name: Plutonium
elements.discoveredBy: Glenn T. Seaborg, Arthur C. Wahl, Joseph W. Kennedy & Edwin McMillan
facts: Named to continue the planetary sequence.
Pu-239 fuels nuclear weapons and some reactors.
First weighed as a visible sample in 1942 at Chicago.

elements.name: Americium
facts: Analog of europium — named for a continent.
Ionization smoke detectors use a tiny Am-241 source.
Synthesized by bombarding plutonium.

elements.name: Curium
facts: Named to honor the Curies.
Used in space RTG research and alpha-particle sources.
Glows purple from its own radioactivity in quantity.

elements.name: Berkelium
facts: Made at the University of California, Berkeley.
Soft, silvery, radioactive metal.
Target material for synthesizing heavier elements.

elements.name: Californium
facts: Powerful neutron emitter for reactors and oil-well logging.
One of the heaviest elements with practical uses.
Named for the state and university.

elements.name: Einsteinium
facts: Found in debris from the first hydrogen bomb test.
Named for Einstein.
Soft, silvery, highly radioactive.

elements.name: Fermium
facts: Also identified in Ivy Mike fallout.
Named for the architect of the nuclear reactor.
No weighable samples — studied atom by atom.

elements.name: Mendelevium
facts: First element identified one atom at a time.
Named for the periodic table's creator.
Made by bombarding einsteinium with helium.

elements.name: Nobelium
facts: Named for the founder of the Nobel Prizes.
Short-lived; chemistry probed with single atoms.
Priority was long contested between labs.

elements.name: Lawrencium
facts: Named for the cyclotron's inventor.
Last actinide — ends the f-block series.
Produced in particle accelerators.

elements.name: Rutherfordium
facts: Named for the father of nuclear physics.
First transactinide; chemistry resembles hafnium.
Half-lives measured in seconds to minutes.

elements.name: Dubnium
facts: Named for the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research town.
Behaves like tantalum in chemical studies.
Made by heavy-ion fusion.

elements.name: Seaborgium
facts: First element named for a living person (Seaborg).
Chemistry akin to tungsten.
Honors the discoverer of many actinides.

elements.name: Bohrium
facts: Named for the quantum pioneer.
Extremely short-lived; few atoms ever made.
Produced by cold fusion of chromium with bismuth.

elements.name: Hassium
facts: Named for the German state of Hesse.
Expected to resemble osmium chemically.
Synthesized at the GSI accelerator.

elements.name: Meitnerium
facts: Honors the co-discoverer of nuclear fission.
No stable isotopes; milliseconds of existence.
One of the rarest human-made elements.

elements.name: Darmstadtium
facts: Named for the city of its discovery lab.
Predicted to be a noble-metal-like element.
Only a handful of atoms observed.

elements.name: Roentgenium
facts: Named for the discoverer of X-rays.
Expected chemistry similar to gold.
Extremely radioactive and fleeting.

elements.name: Copernicium
facts: Named for the heliocentric astronomer.
May be unusually volatile for a metal.
Officially recognized in 2010.

elements.name: Nihonium
facts: First element discovered in Asia.
Name means Japan in Japanese.
Confirmed after years of careful atom counting.

elements.name: Flerovium
facts: Named for the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions.
May show semi-noble gas–like volatility.
Superheavy research cornerstone.

elements.name: Moscovium
facts: Named for the Moscow region.
Produced by calcium-48 beams on americium.
Exists for fractions of a second.

elements.name: Livermorium
facts: Honors the California lab partnership.
Heavier cousin of polonium chemically.
Only a few atoms ever detected.

elements.name: Tennessine
facts: Named for Tennessee and its research institutions.
Heaviest halogen — likely more metallic than iodine.
Synthesized using berkelium targets.

elements.name: Oganesson
facts: Second element named for a living scientist.
Heaviest known element; predicted unusual noble-gas behavior.
Closes period 7 of the table.
